title: Periodisation models: traditional, block, reverse
goal: Describe how traditional, block and reverse periodisation organise a season into macro-, meso- and microcycles, and why Kiely argues the models rest on shaky ground.

steps.title: Cycles inside cycles
steps.text:
[Periodisation](g:periodisation) means splitting a season into smaller planned pieces instead of training the same way all year [[c:per-division]]. Three sizes are used:

| unit | typical length | example |
|---|---|---|
| [macrocycle](g:macrocycle) | a season or year | October to the August A race |
| [mesocycle](g:mesocycle) | 2–6 weeks | a 4-week block of long rides |
| [microcycle](g:microcycle) | about 1 week | Tuesday intervals, Saturday long ride, Monday off |

The words are only labels: they say nothing yet about *what* goes in each piece. The models in this lesson differ in how they fill and order them.

claims.text: Traditional periodisation divides the season into smaller periods and training units.

evidence.quote: At that time, traditional 'training periodization', a division of the entire seasonal programme into smaller periods and training units, was proposed and elucidated.

steps.title: Traditional (linear) periodisation

claims.text: Issurin lists the limits of traditional periodisation: conflicting responses to mixed training, accumulated fatigue, diluted stimulus, and poor support for several peaks in a season.

evidence.quote: (ii) excessive fatigue elicited by prolonged periods of multi-targeted training; (iii) insufficient training stimulation induced by workloads of medium and low concentration typical of 'mixed' training; and (iv) the inability to provide multi-peak performances over the season.

steps.title: Block periodisation
steps.text:
[Block periodisation](g:block-periodisation) puts highly concentrated work on just a few abilities into one block, then moves to the next ability [[c:per-block-idea]]. Two versions exist:

- **Issurin's**: mesocycles of a few weeks, each on a small set of abilities, in a fixed order (build, then convert, then race).
- **Scandinavian HIT blocks** (Rønnestad's group): a week with about 5 [HIIT](g:hiit) sessions, then 3 weeks with 1 HIIT session a week and mostly easy riding.

The 2019 meta-analysis counted any block of at least one week with one concentrated focus [[c:per-block-define]]. The total hours and total intervals can be the same as a traditional plan: only their order changes.

claims.text: Block periodisation sequences specialised blocks of concentrated work on a minimal number of targeted abilities.

evidence.quote: Its general idea proposes the sequencing of specialized training cycles, i.e. blocks, which contain highly concentrated workloads directed to a minimal number of targeted abilities.

claims.text: The block meta-analysis counted one or more blocks of at least a week of concentrated focus as block periodisation.

evidence.quote: In this paper, we define BP training as either one or more blocks with ≥1 week duration of concentrated training focus with either a uni- or multitargeted approach, which means that both BP models are included.

steps.title: Reverse periodisation
steps.text:
[Reverse periodisation](g:reverse-periodisation) flips the traditional order: short, hard, low-volume training dominates early, then volume rises a little while intensity is kept as the season goes on [[c:per-reverse-define]]. Much of the research on it is in swimmers, with some in runners and triathletes.

A systematic review of 11 small studies (200 recreational and trained athletes) found it no better than traditional or block plans for performance or [VO2max](g:vo2max) [[c:per-reverse-result]]. In one study of 32 amateur triathletes, a 4 + 4 week plan with a 2-week taper worked about equally in either order.

claims.text: In reverse periodisation, high-intensity, low-volume training dominates the preparation period, then volume rises slightly while intensity is kept.

evidence.quote: reverse periodization, where in contrast to traditional periodization, high-intensity low-volume training predominates during the preparatory period, before the volume is increased slightly, and intensity is maintained as the season progresses.

claims.text: Reverse periodisation has not been shown to beat traditional or block periodisation.

evidence.quote: Reverse periodization does not provide superior performance improvements in swimming, running, muscular endurance, maximum strength, or maximal oxygen uptake, compared to traditional or block periodization.

Finally, reverse and traditional periodization were an effective strategy to improve running biomechanical, performance, and physiological variables, as well as efficient periodization strategies to improve swimming technical ability, aerobic, and anaerobic swimming performance.

steps.title: The concept vs the evidence: Kiely's critique
steps.text:
Kiely argues that the classic models grew out of coaching tradition and early stress science (Hans Selye: the body gives the same stereotyped answer to any stress). Some of those founding ideas are no longer scientifically defensible, yet they still shape the plans [[c:per-kiely-tradition]].

What replaced them: responses to the same training vary widely between people [[c:per-kiely-variation]], and stress from work, sleep and life changes how you adapt. So, he says, no generic formula can say in advance what week 9 should hold [[c:per-kiely-no-formula]].

His advice isn't to drop planning. Keep a rough plan with clear goals, and adjust it often to what you see in the athlete.

claims.text: Kiely argues that periodisation models rest partly on assumptions that are no longer scientifically justifiable.

evidence.quote: A concern with certain of these formative assumptions is that, although no longer scientifically justifiable, their shaping influence remains deeply embedded.

claims.text: Training responses vary widely between individuals, depending on many factors.

evidence.quote: In recent years substantial evidence has emerged demonstrating that training responses vary extensively, depending upon multiple underlying factors.

claims.text: There is no generic formula that fixes the right plan in advance.

evidence.quote: contemporary evidence compellingly illustrates that there are no generalized formulaic solutions to these planning puzzles.

debate.question: Are periodisation models a sound basis for planning, or tradition dressed up as science?

sides.position: Structured models give coaches useful guidelines; block periodisation fixes the known weak points of the traditional model.
The models rest on outdated stress theory and assume predictable responses; plan loosely and steer by the athlete's response.

points: Periodisation splits a season into macrocycles (season), mesocycles (2–6 weeks) and microcycles (about a week).
Traditional: lots of volume first, intensity later, many abilities trained together; weak at several peaks a season.
Block: concentrated focus on a few abilities per block (e.g. a week of 5 HIIT sessions), in sequence, often at the same total load.
Reverse: intensity first, volume later; no better than the others in small studies.
Kiely: the models rest on old assumptions; responses vary, so plan loosely and adjust.

variants.stem: What is the name for a 2–6-week piece of a training plan with one main aim?

options.text: A mesocycle
options.why: Right: the middle unit, between the season and the week.

options.text: A microcycle
options.why: A microcycle is shorter: usually one week of sessions.

options.text: A macrocycle
options.why: A macrocycle is the whole season or year.

options.text: A taper
options.why: A taper is the short cut-back before a race, not a general unit of the plan.

variants.stem: A runner's plan for a spring marathon says: "Every week: Tuesday track session, Thursday tempo, Sunday long run." Which unit of the plan is this repeating pattern?

options.text: A microcycle
options.why: Right: the repeating week of sessions is the microcycle.

options.text: A mesocycle
options.why: A mesocycle is several of these weeks grouped around one aim.

options.text: A macrocycle
options.why: The macrocycle is the whole build to the marathon, not one week.

options.text: A block
options.why: A block is a mesocycle with one concentrated focus, not a weekly pattern.

variants.stem: A triathlete's coach writes: "Weeks 5–8: build bike volume from 6 to 9 hours." Which unit of the plan is this?

options.text: A mesocycle
options.why: Right: a few weeks with one main aim is a mesocycle.

options.text: A microcycle
options.why: A microcycle is a single week; this spans four.

options.text: A macrocycle
options.why: The macrocycle is the whole season to the main race.

options.text: A recovery week
options.why: There's no easing here; volume is building.

variants.stem: How do volume and intensity change across a season in traditional (linear) periodisation?

options.text: Volume high early then falls; intensity low early then rises
options.why: Right: the classic shape trades volume for intensity as the race nears.

options.text: Intensity high early then falls; volume rises later
options.why: That is reverse periodisation.

options.text: Both stay constant; only the type of session changes
options.why: Traditional plans do change volume and intensity across the season.

options.text: Each block trains one ability at a time
options.why: That is block periodisation; traditional plans train many abilities at once.

variants.stem: A road cyclist has three important races spread over May to August and follows one long traditional plan that builds to a single peak in August. Which weakness of the traditional model, as listed by Issurin, hits her hardest?

options.text: It is built for one peak and copes badly with several
options.why: Right: Issurin lists the inability to provide several peaks in a season.

options.text: It has too little easy volume early in the season
options.why: Traditional plans put lots of easy volume early; that is their defining feature.

options.text: It trains only one ability at a time
options.why: That describes block periodisation; traditional training is mixed.

options.text: It skips the taper before the final race
options.why: Traditional plans include a taper; the issue is the number of peaks.

variants.stem: Which of these plans for a triathlete is block periodisation?

options.text: Week 1: five bike interval sessions; weeks 2–4: one interval session a week, rest easy
options.why: Right: a concentrated week of one focus, then a different emphasis, is a HIT block.

options.text: Every week for 12 weeks: two interval sessions plus easy training
options.why: Spreading intervals evenly every week is the traditional organisation.

options.text: Months 1–3 high volume, months 4–6 more intensity, done gradually
options.why: A gradual volume-to-intensity shift is traditional periodisation.

options.text: Months 1–2 mostly intervals at low volume, then more volume
options.why: Intensity first then volume is reverse periodisation.

variants.stem: In the block vs traditional cycling trials, both groups did the same total hours and the same number of interval sessions. What differed?

options.text: How the intervals were spread over weeks
options.why: Right: only their distribution changed, concentrated in one week or spread evenly.

options.text: How hard each interval was
options.why: Both groups did intervals at similar high intensity; what changed was their timing.

options.text: How many total hours were ridden
options.why: The groups were matched for total volume.

options.text: Which sport they trained
options.why: All were cyclists training on the bike.

variants.stem: A 5 km runner plans: October–December short hill sprints and fast intervals at low mileage; January–March more mileage, keeping the fast sessions. Which model is this?

options.text: Reverse periodisation
options.why: Right: intensity first, volume added later, intensity kept.

options.text: Traditional periodisation
options.why: Traditional plans start with high volume and add intensity later.

options.text: Block periodisation
options.why: Blocks concentrate on one ability in turn; this is a slow intensity-to-volume shift.

options.text: No periodisation
options.why: There are clear planned phases, so it is periodised.

variants.stem: What did the 2022 systematic review conclude about reverse periodisation?

options.text: It was no better than traditional or block plans
options.why: Right: across 11 small studies it gave no extra performance benefit.

options.text: It was clearly better for endurance events
options.why: The review found no superiority in swimming, running or VO2max.

options.text: It harmed performance compared with no plan
options.why: Both reverse and traditional plans improved performance in the studies.

options.text: It could not be studied, as no trials exist
options.why: There were 11 studies with 200 athletes, though small.

variants.stem: What is the core of Kiely's critique of periodisation models?

options.text: They assume everyone adapts on a predictable path, which is false
options.why: Right: responses vary widely, so a generic formula can't fix the plan in advance.

options.text: They contain too much high-intensity training
options.why: Kiely's critique is about planning logic, not the amount of intensity.

options.text: Planning training is useless and should stop
options.why: He keeps planning, but argues for loose plans that adapt.

options.text: They ignore the taper before races
options.why: His concern is the founding assumptions, not tapering.

variants.stem: A cyclist's coach says: "Follow my 16-week plan exactly and you'll peak on race day." In week 7 the rider has a stressful house move and sleeps badly. What fits Kiely's view best?

options.text: Change the week to what the rider can absorb, keeping the end goal
options.why: Right: life stress changes adaptation; plans should steer by the athlete's response.

options.text: Do the planned week; the plan's timing is what makes the peak
options.why: That assumes a fixed, predictable response, which Kiely argues is false.

options.text: Drop the plan and train by feel for the rest of the season
options.why: Kiely keeps a goal-directed plan; he doesn't argue for no plan.

options.text: Add load to make up for the stress
options.why: Extra stress on top of life stress raises the risk of poor adaptation.
